lead: An optical receiver turns a weak stream of photons into clean bits. This unit shows how a photodiode converts light into current, how much noise that current carries, and how much optical power a receiver needs before the bit error rate becomes too high. After it you can compute responsivity, choose between PIN and APD, and work out a receiver's sensitivity in dBm.
about: The unit moves from a single photon to a finished bit decision. Chapter 4.1 fixes the conversion rate: quantum efficiency η and responsivity R turn optical power into current. Chapter 4.2 builds the PN and PIN photodiode that collects those carriers, and shows the efficiency-versus-speed trade-off set by the depletion width. Chapter 4.3 adds gain with the avalanche photodiode, and its price, the excess noise factor. Chapter 4.4 counts the noise sources, shot and thermal, that set the floor. Chapter 4.5 puts photodiode, preamplifier, filter and decision circuit together and defines sensitivity. Chapter 4.6 turns the noise numbers into a Q factor and a bit error rate, and shows what a power penalty is worth in decibels.

chapters.idea: A photodiode converts light to current at a fixed rate: η says how many photons produce collected electrons, and R = ηqλ/hc packs that into amperes per watt.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach detection principles as a separate topic; most fold it into the photodiode chapter. Define photon energy E = hν = hc/λ, with h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, λ in metres. Incident power P watts means P/hν photons per second. Quantum efficiency η = electrons collected ÷ photons incident, including the fraction (1 − R) not reflected at the facet. Primary photocurrent I_ph = ηqP/hν, with q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Responsivity R = I_ph/P = ηqλ/(hc) = ηλ/1.24 when λ is in micrometres, in A/W. Show that R cannot exceed λ/1.24, and that R falls to zero past the bandgap wavelength λ_c = 1.24/E_g with E_g in eV. Some syllabi spell it 'responsivity' and some 'quantum efficiency and responsivity' as two marks.

figure.aria: Two straight lines of responsivity against wavelength in micrometres, one for quantum efficiency 1 and one for 0.8, both rising with wavelength and separated by a constant factor.

chapters.example: A silicon PIN photodiode has quantum efficiency η = 0.8 at λ = 0.85 µm and receives P = 1 µW. Find R, the photon rate and the photocurrent. Photon energy hc/λ = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10⁸)/(0.85 × 10⁻⁶) = 2.34 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Photon rate = 1 × 10⁻⁶/2.34 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.27 × 10¹² per second. Collected electrons = 0.8 × 4.27 × 10¹² = 3.42 × 10¹² per second, so I_ph = 3.42 × 10¹² × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 0.547 µA. Check with the formula: R = 0.8 × 0.85/1.24 = 0.548 A/W, and I_ph = 0.548 × 1 µW = 0.548 µA. The two answers agree.
chapters.trap: Putting λ in metres into R = ηλ/1.24, or confusing η (a pure ratio, no units) with R (A/W). A second trap is claiming R can be raised past λ/1.24 by better design; that is the hard ceiling at η = 1.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 on photon energy, bandgap and absorption, since η depends on how strongly the material absorbs at that wavelength.
chapters.leave: Junction structure and depletion width to 4.2, gain to 4.3, noise to 4.4.

chapters.idea: A reverse-biased junction sweeps light-made carriers out as current, and widening the depleted i layer of a PIN raises efficiency while slowing the carrier transit.
chapters.depth: Start from a reverse-biased PN junction: photons absorbed inside the depletion region create electron-hole pairs that the field sweeps out as drift current; pairs made outside it diffuse slowly and often recombine. Quantum efficiency of a front-illuminated diode: η = (1 − R)(1 − e^(−αw)), with α the absorption coefficient in m⁻¹ and w the depletion width in metres. Junction capacitance C = εA/w, with ε = ε_rε₀, A the area, so a thin PN layer gives high C and a wide PIN gives low C. Transit time t = w/v_sat with v_sat the saturation drift velocity (about 1 × 10⁵ m/s in Si, 6.5 × 10⁴ m/s in InGaAs). Two bandwidth limits: transit-time f ≈ 0.4/t and RC f = 1/(2πR_L C); the smaller one wins. Cover the PIN layer stack, antireflection coating, and typical material bands: Si for 0.85 µm, Ge and InGaAs for 1.3 and 1.55 µm, with R around 0.5–0.6 A/W for Si and about 0.9 A/W for InGaAs at 1.55 µm.

figure.title: Front-illuminated PIN photodiode
figure.aria: Vertical stack from incoming light through antireflection coating, thin p+ layer, wide undoped i layer where pairs are swept, n+ layer, and the load resistor that receives the photocurrent.

chapters.example: An InGaAs PIN photodiode has depletion width w = 4 µm, absorption coefficient α = 1 × 10⁴ cm⁻¹ at 1.55 µm, facet reflectivity R = 0.03, area A = 1 × 10⁻⁸ m², ε_r = 13.9, and works into R_L = 50 Ω. Find η, the transit time, and both bandwidth limits. αw = 1 × 10⁴ cm⁻¹ × 4 × 10⁻⁴ cm = 4, so e^(−4) = 0.0183 and η = 0.97 × (1 − 0.0183) = 0.952. Transit time t = 4 × 10⁻⁶/6.5 × 10⁴ = 6.15 × 10⁻¹¹ s = 61.5 ps, giving f ≈ 0.4/t = 6.5 GHz. Capacitance C = (13.9 × 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 1 × 10⁻⁸)/(4 × 10⁻⁶) = 3.08 × 10⁻¹³ F = 0.31 pF, so 1/(2πR_L C) = 10.3 GHz. Transit time limits the diode.
chapters.trap: Assuming a thicker i layer is always better. It raises η but lengthens the transit time and the diode slows down. Also forgetting the (1 − R) reflection factor, which costs about 3% even with a good coating.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1 for η and R, and Unit 1 for how light propagates and is absorbed in a semiconductor is not needed here, but Unit 3 for absorption in direct-bandgap material helps.
chapters.leave: Multiplication to 4.3, noise to 4.4, and how the diode sits inside a full receiver to 4.5.

chapters.idea: An APD multiplies each primary pair by impact ionisation; gain M raises the signal by M but the shot noise by M²F, so there is an optimum M.
chapters.depth: Explain the high-field multiplication region near breakdown: a carrier accelerated over the ionisation threshold knocks out a new pair, and the process repeats. Gain M = I_M/I_ph, typically 10 to 100, with M = 1/(1 − (V/V_B)^n) as a usable empirical form, V_B the breakdown voltage and n a fitting number around 3 to 6. The randomness of the process adds the excess noise factor F(M) = kM + (2 − 1/M)(1 − k), where k is the ratio of hole to electron ionisation rates. Signal power grows as M², shot noise as M²F, so SNR improves only until F catches up; that gives an optimum M. Low k means low noise: silicon has small k and is used at 0.85 µm; InGaAs absorbs at 1.3–1.55 µm but multiplies poorly, so the separate absorption and multiplication (SAM) structure with an InP gain layer is used. Bias is far higher than a PIN and needs temperature control. Mention the gain-bandwidth product for speed.

figure.title: Avalanche multiplication
figure.aria: Flow from absorbed photon to primary pair, into the high-field region, through impact ionisation and secondary pairs, with a dashed loop back to ionisation that repeats before the multiplied current leaves.

chapters.example: An APD has η = 0.8 at λ = 1.3 µm, gain M = 10, ionisation ratio k = 0.3, and receives P = 100 nW in a 1 GHz bandwidth. Find the multiplied current, the excess noise factor and the SNR. R = 0.8 × 1.3/1.24 = 0.839 A/W, so I_ph = 0.839 × 100 × 10⁻⁹ = 83.9 nA and I_M = M I_ph = 0.839 µA. F = kM + (2 − 1/M)(1 − k) = 0.3 × 10 + (2 − 0.1)(0.7) = 3 + 1.33 = 4.33. Shot noise <i²> = 2q I_ph M² F B = 2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 83.9 × 10⁻⁹ × 100 × 4.33 × 10⁹ = 1.16 × 10⁻¹⁴ A², so the rms noise is 108 nA. SNR = (0.839 × 10⁻⁶)²/1.16 × 10⁻¹⁴ = 60.7, that is 17.8 dB.
chapters.trap: Multiplying only the signal and forgetting the excess noise: noise grows as M²F, not M². Another trap is saying a bigger M always helps; past the optimum M the added noise beats the added gain.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2 for the primary photocurrent and the absorption region, and Unit 3 for carrier behaviour in a strongly reverse-biased junction.
chapters.leave: The comparison with PIN receiver sensitivity belongs to 4.5 and 4.6, where the full noise sum is available.

chapters.idea: Two noises set the floor of every receiver: shot noise from the random arrival of photocurrent and dark-current carriers, and thermal noise from the load resistor.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach photodetector noise as a stand-alone topic. Shot noise comes from carriers arriving randomly, a Poisson process: <i_sh²> = 2q(I_ph + I_d)B, with q the electron charge, I_d the dark current and B the post-detection bandwidth in hertz. Dark current has a bulk part (proportional to depleted volume) and a surface part (leakage), and both are multiplied by M in an APD. Thermal or Johnson noise in the load resistor: <i_th²> = 4kTB/R_L, with k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K, T in kelvin, R_L in ohms. Add them: σ² = <i_sh²> + <i_th²>, then SNR = I_ph²/σ², quoted in dB as 10 log₁₀ of the ratio. Under the thermal limit SNR rises as P², that is 20 dB per decade of power; under the shot limit it rises as P, 10 dB per decade. Give one line each to 1/f noise and to noise equivalent power, NEP = σ_rms/R in W per root hertz, and mention that a larger R_L lowers thermal noise but narrows the bandwidth.

figure.title: Noise sources at the photodiode
figure.aria: Two noise branches, shot noise from the diode current and thermal noise from the load resistor, joining into a total noise block that gives the output signal-to-noise ratio.

chapters.example: A PIN receiver has R = 0.8 A/W, receives P = 1 µW, has dark current I_d = 1 nA, bandwidth B = 100 MHz, load R_L = 1 kΩ at T = 300 K. Find each noise current and the SNR. I_ph = 0.8 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.8 µA, so I_ph + I_d = 0.801 µA. Shot noise <i²> = 2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.801 × 10⁻⁶ × 1 × 10⁸ = 2.56 × 10⁻¹⁷ A², rms 5.06 nA. Thermal noise <i²> = 4 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 300 × 1 × 10⁸/1000 = 1.66 × 10⁻¹⁵ A², rms 40.7 nA. Total = 1.68 × 10⁻¹⁵ A², rms 41 nA. SNR = (0.8 × 10⁻⁶)²/1.68 × 10⁻¹⁵ = 381, that is 25.8 dB. The receiver is thermal-noise limited.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that both noise powers add and not the rms currents. A second trap is thinking a bigger R_L always helps: it cuts thermal noise but also cuts the bandwidth, so the receiver must be redesigned, not just re-resistored.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2 for I_ph and capacitance, chapter 4.3 for the excess noise factor in the APD case.
chapters.leave: How the amplifier adds its own noise and how the whole receiver is specified goes to 4.5; turning noise into an error rate goes to 4.6.

chapters.idea: A receiver is a photodiode, a low-noise front end, a filter and a decision circuit, and its sensitivity is the weakest average power that still meets the target error rate.
chapters.depth: Draw the chain: photodiode, preamplifier, main amplifier and equaliser, low-pass filter, decision circuit fed by a recovered clock; add AGC as a control loop. Cover the three front ends and their trade-offs: low impedance (wide band, noisy), high impedance (quiet, narrow band, needs equalisation), and transimpedance with feedback resistor R_f, where transresistance is set by R_f and the bandwidth by R_f and the input capacitance. Define sensitivity as the minimum average received power at a stated bit rate and a stated BER, always in dBm: P_dBm = 10 log₁₀(P/1 mW). For a thermal-noise-limited PIN receiver with equal noise on ones and zeros, P ≈ Qσ/R with Q the factor from 4.6, and Q ≈ 6 for 10⁻⁹. Practical PIN receivers land in the −25 to −40 dBm region at a few hundred Mbit/s. Mention dynamic range, overload and that an APD buys roughly 5 to 10 dB at the cost of a bias supply and temperature drift.

figure.title: Digital optical receiver
figure.aria: Receiver chain from photodiode through preamplifier, main amplifier and filter, into the decision circuit that also receives a recovered clock, and out as data.

chapters.example: A PIN receiver has responsivity R = 0.9 A/W and a total input noise current of 40 nA rms, and must reach BER 10⁻⁹, which needs Q = 6. Find the sensitivity in watts and dBm. P = Qσ/R = 6 × 40 × 10⁻⁹/0.9 = 2.67 × 10⁻⁷ W = 267 nW. In dBm: 10 log₁₀(267 × 10⁻⁹/1 × 10⁻³) = 10 log₁₀(2.67 × 10⁻⁴) = −35.7 dBm. If the link budget loses 30 dB, the transmitter must launch at least −35.7 + 30 = −5.7 dBm of average power.
chapters.trap: Quoting a sensitivity number alone. It means nothing without the bit rate and the BER it was measured at, and datasheets sometimes quote peak power where the formula uses average power.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.4 for the noise current, chapter 4.2 for responsivity; Unit 5 uses this sensitivity directly in the link power budget.
chapters.leave: The Q factor and the exact BER curve go to 4.6; the rise-time side of the budget is Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Bit error rate is just the probability that noise pushes a sample across the decision threshold, and it is fixed by one number, Q = (I₁ − I₀)/(σ₁ + σ₀).
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this as a separate chapter. Model the received samples as Gaussian around means I₁ and I₀ with rms noises σ₁ and σ₀, threshold midway. Then Q = (I₁ − I₀)/(σ₁ + σ₀) and BER = ½ erfc(Q/√2) ≈ (1/√(2π))·e^(−Q²/2)/Q for Q above about 3. Standard anchor points: Q = 6 gives BER ≈ 10⁻⁹, Q = 7 gives about 10⁻¹², Q = 4.5 gives about 10⁻⁶. Show the eye diagram as the picture of the same thing, with eye opening and eye closure, and mention that timing jitter and intersymbol interference close the eye. Power penalty in dB = 10 log₁₀(P₂/P₁) = 20 log₁₀(Q₂/Q₁) when noise is unchanged. One line on the extinction-ratio penalty and one on a BER floor caused by noise that is not Gaussian.

figure.aria: A near-straight falling line of log base ten of bit error rate against the Q factor, reaching about minus nine at Q equal to six and about minus twelve at Q equal to seven.

chapters.example: A receiver gives I₁ = 1.0 µA and I₀ = 0.10 µA with equal noise σ₁ = σ₀ = 0.075 µA. Find Q, the BER, and the extra power needed to reach 10⁻¹². Q = (1.0 − 0.10)/(0.075 + 0.075) = 0.90/0.15 = 6.0, so BER ≈ 10⁻⁹. For BER 10⁻¹² we need Q = 7.03. With responsivity fixed, power scales with Q, so the penalty is 20 log₁₀(7.03/6.0) = 20 log₁₀(1.172) = 1.38 dB. The transmitter must deliver about 1.4 dB more average power, or the receiver must be 1.4 dB quieter.
chapters.trap: Using only σ₁ or only σ₀ in the denominator. Q uses their sum. A second trap is quoting BER without the bit rate, and forgetting that an APD's noise depends on the signal, so σ₁ and σ₀ are genuinely different.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.4 for σ, chapter 4.5 for how sensitivity relates to Q.
chapters.leave: System-level penalties from dispersion and jitter over a real link belong to Unit 5 and Unit 2.
